title: Hashimoto Thyroiditis
subject: Pathology
summary: Hashimoto thyroiditis is a chronic autoimmune destruction of the thyroid, most common cause of hypothyroidism in iodine‑sufficient areas. It presents with a firm, rubbery gland and fluctuating thyroid function.

sections.p: A lymphocytic infiltrate with germinal centres destroys follicular cells. Diagnosis rests on anti‑TPO/anti‑TG antibodies and a normal or enlarged gland on palpation.

t.b: Presence confirms autoimmune thyroiditis; >100 IU/mL strongly suggests Hashimoto
Elevated in hypothyroid phase; low in transient hyperthyroidism
Low in hypothyroid phase; may be normal or high in early hyperthyroid phase

sections.p: Staging is functional: euthyroid, transient hyperthyroid (Hashitoxicosis), overt hypothyroid. Histologically, early stages show lymphoid aggregates; late stages show fibrosis and atrophy.
Autoimmune attack mediated by CD8+ T cells and anti‑TPO antibodies. Risk factors include female sex, age 30‑50, family history, and other autoimmune diseases.
Patients complain of fatigue, weight gain, cold intolerance, constipation, and menstrual irregularity. Neck exam shows a firm, non‑tender, rubbery gland.
In low‑resource settings, focus on TSH, free T4, and anti‑TPO if available. Ultrasound can assess gland size and echogenicity.
Rapidly enlarging goitre, compressive symptoms, or unexplained weight loss may signal lymphoma. Persistent hyperthyroidism can lead to atrial fibrillation.
Treat hypothyroidism with levothyroxine. Monitor TSH every 6–8 weeks until stable. Avoid antithyroid drugs unless hyperthyroid phase is severe.
b: Avoid antithyroid drugs in hypothyroid phase

sections.p: Annual TSH and free T4 in stable patients. Counsel on iodine intake and avoid unnecessary iodine supplements.
Hashimoto can mimic subacute thyroiditis, Graves’ disease, and thyroid lymphoma.
b: Subacute thyroiditis – painful gland, elevated ESR
Thyroid lymphoma – rapidly enlarging, firm, compressive

sections.p: TSH may be normal in early Hashitoxicosis; anti‑TPO can be negative in early disease. Ultrasound may show normal size in early stages.
b: Normal TSH in early hyperthyroid phase

faq.a: Yes, transient hyperthyroidism (Hashitoxicosis) occurs early due to follicular cell destruction releasing hormone.
Excess iodine can precipitate or worsen Hashimoto; use only if deficiency is proven.

faq.q: What is the risk of lymphoma?
faq.a: About 1–2% of patients develop thyroid lymphoma, usually after many years of chronic disease.

exam: A 35‑year‑old woman presents with fatigue and weight gain. TSH is 6.5 mIU/L, free T4 low, anti‑TPO positive. What is the next step? — Start levothyroxine and repeat TSH in 6–8 weeks.
A patient with Hashimoto develops rapid goitre enlargement. What is the most likely complication? — Thyroid lymphoma; urgent ultrasound and referral.
A 28‑year‑old man has a firm, non‑tender goitre and TSH 0.5 mIU/L. Which diagnosis is most likely? — Hashitoxicosis; consider antithyroid drugs only if severe.
You have a patient with Hashimoto and atrial fibrillation. What is the priority? — Treat the arrhythmia and consider thyroid hormone replacement.
A patient with Hashimoto has normal TSH but feels fatigued. What should you investigate? — Repeat free T4 and anti‑TPO; consider early hyperthyroid phase.
You are in a rural clinic without anti‑TPO testing. How do you diagnose Hashimoto? — Use clinical features, TSH, free T4, and ultrasound if available.
A patient with Hashimoto is pregnant. What is the safest treatment? — Levothyroxine; avoid antithyroid drugs unless hyperthyroid.
